title: Testing the project's own checking machinery only on the author's machine hides defects
body:
## What goes wrong

The checks that enforce this project's rules were developed and run on one person's
laptop, where they passed. Within about fifty minutes of first running anywhere else,
they exposed two defects, neither of which was visible locally and one of which would
have blocked the project entirely.

The first: `polymath publish` died with a raw `Author identity unknown` error from inside
git, after having written the record, created a branch and staged the files. Every new
member would have hit this at their first publication, because git on macOS guesses an
identity from the account name and hostname while other machines refuse to guess. The
author's machine was configured, by accident of history, in the one way that conceals the
problem.

The second: the pull-request workflow ran the *accepted* branch's test suite rather than
the proposal's. A failing test on the accepted branch therefore blocked every pull
request, including the one that fixed that test. This could not appear until a pull
request existed, which was not until the tooling was already in use.

The sharpest part is not either defect but what happened when the first one was chased.
Two deliberate attempts were made to reproduce it locally by simulating the foreign
environment: the whole suite was run on a purpose-built case-sensitive filesystem, to
catch anything the author's case-insensitive disk was hiding, and again with the git
configuration stripped away. Both passed cleanly, and both hypotheses were wrong.
Simulating the other machine did not work. Only the other machine worked.

This bears directly on the design of the project rather than being incidental to it. The
architecture rests on the automatic checks being the single point of enforcement, on the
grounds that running the client is optional and anything it does can be bypassed. If the
checks themselves are only ever exercised where they were written, that single point of
enforcement is the least tested component in the system.

A secondary lesson: both defects were in the infrastructure, not the mathematics, and a
corpus that records only mathematics teaches its members that this kind of finding is not
worth writing down. It is, and this record exists partly to say so.
author: danny
what_was_tried:
The full test suite was run repeatedly on the author's machine throughout development,
finishing at 168 tests passing, and was treated as evidence that the tooling worked.

When the automatic checks failed on their first run elsewhere, the failure was chased
locally rather than by reading the remote output, which was not accessible without
administrator rights. Two environment differences were hypothesised and tested directly:
a case-sensitive filesystem, created as a disk image for the purpose, since one test had
never executed on the author's case-insensitive disk; and a missing git identity,
simulated by clearing the home directory and both git configuration paths. Each
reproduced cleanly, at 163 tests passing, and each hypothesis was therefore rejected.

The failure was identified only by obtaining the actual output from the run on the other
machine. The correct first move would have been to read that output rather than to
reason about what might differ.
